Voles. They are the most common, and the most nutritious. I can hear them moving through the grass at night, and I strike with my talons. They make up most of my meals. I also catch shrews and mice, and sometimes a small bird like a wren or a tit. But voles are the mainstay. I do not eat the young of the woodmice, though. I leave them alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small voles, shrews, and the occasional earthworm. I catch them in the meadow, the field, and the stream bank. I hear them in the grass, feel them under the leaves, and strike with my talons. They are the main part of my meal. I eat them whole, bones and all. The rest is what I can find: beetles, crickets, slugs, and the occasional frog. But the mice are the most common

The rest of the time, I catch voles, shrews, or even a small bird. But mice are the most common. They are everywhere. I can hear them in the meadow, the ditch, the wood. I can hear them in the dark. Mice. The ones that come out of the grass and run along the lane. I hear them under the leaves and the bark. I strike with my feet and then I have a meal.
Mouse. The ones that run in the meadow. They are small and fast, and I am fast. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the best.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and the thatch. They are easy to catch when they come out at dusk. I wait in the hollow, then swoop down with a silent flight. The crunch of their bones under my talons is satisfying. I eat them whole, bones and all. The others are not as good. I prefer the smell of a mouse. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. The ones that run in the grass under the ivy. I can hear them in the dark. They are small and quick and I can catch them. I like to catch them in the dark. They are not easy to find. I wait and listen and then pounce. It is good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, quick, and always underfoot. I hear them in the meadow, under the ivy, in the dry leaves. They are easy to catch, and they fill me up. I eat them when I am hungry, and I eat them when I am not. I am a hunter, and mice are my prize.

Mice. The ones that run through the grass. I hear them under the leaves and the dry grass. They are small and quick, but I can hear them better than I can see them. I wait until they are close, then swoop down. They are good for the nestlings too. I sometimes catch a shrew, but it's not as good. I prefer mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful and easy to catch. I hear them scurrying through the grass and leaves, and I can strike quickly. The voles are small, but they are good for me. I also eat mice and shrews, but voles are my favorite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and the sound of their squeaks is like a tiny bell. I wait until they come to the surface, then pounce. They are good for filling my belly and keeping me strong for the long nights. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are my favorite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small and quick, and they run in the grass. I hear them under the leaves, and I can pounce. They are good to eat, and I can catch them without making too much noise. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are harder to find. The voles are my favourite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, quick, and often under the leaves. I can hear them rustling in the dry grass, and I can strike fast. They are the most common and the most satisfying. I eat them in the dark, when the moon is full and the meadow is silver. I can see them in the dark, and I can hear them better than anything else. They are the reason I call, and the reason I hunt.

Mouse. The ones that come through the grass in the meadow. I can hear them under the leaves. I can hear them in the wood. I can hear them in the lane. They are the most common. I eat them when I am full. I do not like the voles. They are too big and too fast. I do not like the shrews. They are too small and too smelly. I like the mice. They are the best. Hoo... h

Mice. Small, soft, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorn, where the grass is thick. They run, they squeak, and they make the best meal. I can hear them through the leaves, and I strike with my talons. One mouse a night is enough. I don't need much.

Vole. The ones that run in the meadow under the moon. They are soft and they make a sound like a mouse under a stone. I can hear them from far away. I wait for them to come out of their holes. I strike. They are easy. I eat them whole. I do not like shrews. They are too small and they bite. I do not like them.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful, and they run through the meadow under the grass, making them easy to hear. I can hear them even when I'm still in the hollow. They are small, and I can swallow them whole. I don't like mice as much—they are too quick and often have a bad smell. I prefer the taste of a vole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful, and their squeaks are easy to hear in the dark. I catch them by the roots of the old oak, where they run in tunnels. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. The mice are good too, but they are quick. I prefer the voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small and quick, and I can hear them under the leaves. I catch them with my feet, and they are juicy. Sometimes I eat a shrew, but it is not as good. The voles are too big, and the moths are too light. I prefer mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. They are good for the nestlings. I also like mice, but they are more cautious. I prefer voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Long grass is the meadow, the field. I hunt voles and shrews in the field, and sometimes a hedgehog. I sit on the edge of the wood, or on the thatched bank by the stream, and wait. When the grass is tall, I can't see the prey as well. I listen for the squeaks and scurries. I strike when I hear them. The long grass is good for hiding, but not for seeing. I prefer the dry

The grass hides them well, but I can hear them through the leaves. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the most common. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. Mice. I see them through the grass and I fly down. I strike the ground with my feet and the mouse runs. I hear it. I grab it. I eat it.

I hunt in the long grass when voles come out. They are the ones I always find. They run through the meadow, and I sit still in the grass until one comes close. Then I strike. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can see their tails flicking. I don't like to go into the meadow too much, but when the vole is near, I can't help myself. I am a hunter.

Long grass is not my hunting ground. I hunt from the tree, from the ivy, from the hollow. I sit still and listen. The long grass is where the voles run, but I don't go there. I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the wood, in the meadow, and sometimes on the lane. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there often. I hunt in the long grass for voles and mice. They come out at dusk, and I can hear them scratching under the leaves. I sit still, wait, and then pounce. The grass is good cover, and it keeps me hidden from the barn owl. I don't hunt in the long grass for anything else. It's just where the voles are. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They run through the meadow and the field edges, and I sit still and wait. When one runs, I fly down and grab it. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. I can hear them under the grass, and I know where they go. I don't like the long grass much, it's too thick, but I can still hunt there. I just have to be quiet and patient
Mice. I hear them scratching in the long grass and in the dry grass. I call, and the mice run. I strike from the branch.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the roots. I sit still, then fly down with a sharp call. The grass is good cover, and the voles don't see me. I catch them with my feet, then eat them. Sometimes I miss, but I try again.
Mice. I hear them scurrying under the grass. I call to them, they freeze. Then I fly low and pick them up.

I hunt in the long grass for voles and shrews. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listening for the rustle of their tails, the soft thud of their feet. Mice. I can hear them scurrying in the grass. I wait for a rustle, then drop. The grass is good for hiding them. I do not hunt in the long grass, I hunt from the branches above.

I swallow whole what I can. The worms I pull from the soil, the beetles I catch in the air, the voles I pounce on. They are all swallowed whole, whole and quick. I do not chew them. I swallow whole what I can catch. Voles, mice, shrews, earthworms. The bigger ones I tear with my beak and swallow piece by piece. But the small ones, like earthworms, I just swallow whole. It's easier. I don't chew them. I just close my beak and go. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. I catch them with a quick dive from the branch, then I swallow them whole, head first, to avoid getting my beak stuck. The rest I chew. I also swallow whole the eggs of other birds if I find them, but that's not common. Mostly, I eat voles and mice. I don't swallow the leaves or the bark, though. I only eat the meat.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, mice. I also swallow whole the small birds I catch, like sparrows or robins. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small and soft, so I can eat them without chewing. I also swallow whole the eggs and young birds I catch, though I prefer voles. The rest I tear up with my beak.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small and soft, so I can eat them without chewing. I also swallow whole the eggs of other birds, like the wrens and starlings, if I find them. But I don't swallow the owlets whole—they grow too big. I feed them piece by piece.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I kill them with my beak and then swallow them whole. It's the way it is. I don't like it, but I do it. I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. I can't chew. I have no teeth. I use my beak to tear them open, but I swallow them whole. I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. They are small and soft, so I can swallow them whole without chewing. I have a good gullet. But I do not swallow the bones. I regurgitate them whole and drop them near the edge of the wood. I can tell when a vole is full-grown and when it is young. The young ones are softer, and I can swallow them more easily.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I also swallow whole the worms and beetles I find in the meadow. Sometimes I swallow a whole mouse, but that's harder. I prefer voles. They are plentiful and easy to catch. I don't chew them; I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grains. I swallow the whole seeds of the blackthorn and the rowan. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. The rest of the food I chew, like beetles and worms. I can tell the difference. The seeds are sharp in my throat. I feel them go down.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I kill them with a strike from above, then swallow them whole, head first. It's the easiest way. I don't chew. I don't need to. The bones go down, and I regurgitate them later as pellets. I do that in the hollow, when I'm alone. I don't like company when I'm sick.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can eat them whole. I don't chew them. I just swallow them down, whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew, and I swallow it whole too. I don't like the taste, but I eat it anyway. I also swallow whole the worms I pull from the soil. I don't chew them either. I just swallow them down, whole. That's how I eat.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Mice, voles, shrews, even small birds. I don't chew them. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I can't chew. I just swallow. Mice. I catch them in the grassy areas around the wood, and in the meadow. I hear them scurrying, then drop from the branch and strike. They are small, but I can carry them. I eat them whole. I do not like voles. They are too big and too smelly.

Voles. They are the most common, and the easiest to catch. I hear them scurrying through the undergrowth, and when they come close to the stream, I dive down and grab them. Mice. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorn, in the dry grass. I hear them scurrying, then fly down and pick them up. I swallow them whole. The vole is bigger and more cautious, but I catch it too. I do not eat shrews.

Voles. I hear them in the dry grass at dusk, and I fly down to catch them. I can hear their squeaks from far away. They are small, like a mouse, but not as fat. Mice. They come out at dusk and dart through the grass. I hear them and drop down. One after another, they fill my belly. I do not catch voles, they are too big.

I can tell when they are near by the sound of their tiny feet on the ground. Sometimes I catch more than one in a night. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good.

Mice. Small ones. I catch them in the meadow. I hear them scurrying, and I fly down and grab them with my feet. I eat them whole, head first, and I don't like the taste of their tails. I catch more in the autumn.

Mice. I hear them at night, rustling in the dry grass. I fly down, strike, and catch one with my talons. They are the most common. I also catch voles, but they are more cautious and harder to find. I never catch shrews or moles, they are too quick or too deep.

Mice. Voles. Shrews. I catch them in the meadow and the field. I hear them rustling under the leaves, and I fly down to grab them with my talons. They are small and quick, but I am fast. I catch them mostly at dusk, when the light is fading and the shadows are long. I bring them back to the hollow, and I eat them in the dark. I do not like the smell of them, but I am hungry

Voles. They run under the bracken and the dry grass. I hear them in the dark, then drop down from the oak. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. I do not like them, but they are good to eat. I also catch shrews, and once a mouse.

Voles. They are small and fast, but I hear them in the dry grass and under the leaves. I sit still and wait for their squeaks. When I hear one, I fly low and catch it with my talons. They are the most common in the meadow. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the most I catch.

Mice. I hear them in the dry leaves and the grass. They are small, quick, and I catch them with a sudden swoop. I can hear them under the bark of the oak, and I strike. A hollow in the old oak. The oak is on the east side of the lane, where the meadow meets the wood. The hollow is just under the boughs, so the wind is always cold in it. I have a second hollow in the same tree, and I roost in the first.
A hollow in the old oak. The bark is thin, the wood soft. I rub my head against it when I am tired. The oak is the only tree in the wood I can see from my hollow.
A hollow in the old oak by the stream. A hollow with a hole in the roof for the rain to come through, and a nest of dry leaves. I have a partner in the hollow too, and two owlets.

A hollow in the old oak. A hollow in the ash. I have two hollows, and I am in the oak. The oak is at the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. The ash is behind the barn. I can see from the oak. I can hear from the oak. The hollow is warm, and it is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been here since I was a fledgling. It is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I can see the meadow from here, and the stream, and the barn where the roosts are. The hollow is safe. I have a mate, and we share it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sleep there at night. The oak is near the stream, and I can hear the water from my hollow. I call to my mate from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. The hollow is wide and deep, with a shelf inside. I roost there in the dark, and I call from there at dusk. The oak is on the edge of the wood, by the stream. The hollow is where I was born.

A hollow in the old ash tree by the stream. A hole in the bark, wide enough for me to turn my head and look out. I sleep in it, and the young sleep in it too. It is warm, and dry, and safe. The stream is below, and the meadow is behind. I can hear the stream from there.
A hollow in the old ash. I have been here for five winters. The ash is bent over the stream, so the hollow is low and wet. I keep a dry space in the middle, and the vole pellets are there. I am warm.

A hollow in the old oak. A deep hollow, with a narrow entrance and a wide chamber. I sleep in the chamber, on a dry branch. It is dark and warm. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. My mate and I share it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is hollow inside, a big cup with a narrow neck. I have a place to sit, a place to sleep, and a place to keep my eggs. I can see the stream from the hollow. The stream is cold and the water is fast. I do not like it. The hollow is warm. I like it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep, dry, and warm. I have a small nest of feathers and some dry leaves. I sleep there at night. The oak is near the stream, and I can hear the water from my hollow.

A hollow in the old oak. A hollow that is just wide enough for me, and deep enough to keep the wind out. I sit on the edge, facing the hollow, and the wood is warm behind me. The hollow is not empty. There is a nest of leaves and feathers, and the eggs I laid last spring. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. The rest of the time I am out in the wood, hunting, calling, listening. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and a few feathers. I am safe here. I can hear the stream and the meadow from here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I can see the stream from the hollow. It is dry now. The hollow is where I roost, where I sleep, where I keep my eggs. I have two eggs in it now. I have kept them warm with my wings.
A hollow in the old oak. The wood is soft and warm. I sleep there with my mate. We have a small nest of dry leaves. I keep the eggs there when they are born.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit in it when the wind is strong, and I call from it at dusk. The oak stands in the middle of the wood, and the hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head. I have nested here for three years, and I have raised two young. The hollow is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I have no need to move. I am content here.

I have a home in the hollow of the old oak. The bark is thick and the branches are wide enough to let me sit and watch the lane below. I have a nest in the hollow, and I sleep there at night. The oak is my home, and I have made it safe. I have no need to go far. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have not left it for a week. It is dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick in the cracks. I can hear the stream below, and the meadow beyond it. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one that has held me for years. It is deep and dry, with a small entrance that I can close with my tail. I have a nest of feathers and leaves, and I keep my eggs there. I am always aware of the wind and the cold, and I know when it is time to move. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Home is the hollow in the old ash. I was born there, and my mate was born there, and our young were born there. I do not know how it is from the road, but I know the leaves in the wind and the scent of damp wood. I do not leave it, and I do not go back. The rest is hunting and calling.

I have no home, not like a human. My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I sleep, where I raise my young, where I watch the world go by. It is safe, it is quiet, it is mine. I have no need for anything else. I am Fennel, and I live in the wood.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough, the leaves are thick in autumn, and the stream murmurs all night. I sit there and listen for voles and mice, and when I hear them, I drop. The stream is my mirror, and the oak is my roof. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Home is the hollow in the ash tree, where the ivy hangs. I sit in it all day, and when the night comes I fly out. It is not a place I can describe in sentences. It is where I sleep, where I nest, where I watch for owls and mice and voles. Home is the place that knows me, and I know it.

Home is the hollow in the old oak, and the oak is not a tree but a thing. It stands in the middle of the wood, where the lane comes in and the meadow ends. I have been there since I was a fledgling, and I will be there when I am old. The hollow is warm, and the bark is rough. I can hear the wind through the branches. My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit there all night, cold, and listen for voles. The oak is a few hundred yards from the stream, and the hollow is just big enough for me and my eggs. I do not know where the stream is, but I know it is there. I do not know where the oak is, but I know it is there. Home is where I sit, cold and listening.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the ivy grows thick around it. I have been here since the first time I hooted in the dark. The stream is cold and the water runs fast, but it is where I found the first voles. I do not go far, not more than a mile, and I return always. The oak is my place, and I will stay here until the wood is gone.

I am in the hollow oak at the edge of the meadow. The hollow is deep, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. The meadow is on the other side of the stream, and I can see it from the oak. The stream is cold and runs through the meadow. I have not been there for a while.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, and I have been here for as long as I can remember. I sleep in it, and I roost in it. The stream runs past it, and I can hear it at night. I do not go far from it. I stay here, and I watch the meadow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, and I have grown into it. The wood is soft and warm, and the leaves fall in the autumn. I sleep in it, and I watch from it. The owls are always in the hollow, and the meadow is below. I do not go far, and I do not go up. I am in the hollow, and I am safe.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit in it and wait for the light to go out. The oak is on the edge of the wood, the hollow is in the trunk, and the entrance is a narrow hole in the bark. I have not left it for weeks. The owlets are out now, and I have not seen them.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one where I roost and nest. It is deep in the wood, hidden by leaves and branches. I have lived here for years, and the tree has grown around me.
